universal_lens: Rowing mechanics map to a constrained Hamiltonian system. The keel alignment defines the principal axis of inertia, while the catch and finish dictate impulse transfer. Synchronization errors manifest as phase lags or spatial deviations, generating destructive torque and drag that degrade the collective thrust vector.
gsi_mapping: GSI treats crew synchronization as a time-series coherence problem. Bayesian filters estimate individual oarsman phase states from telemetry. Conformal prediction bounds quantify the probability of 'swinging out' or 'getting in late', dynamically updating the collective efficiency metric based on observed kinematic variance.
gse_mapping: GSE models the shell as a multi-agent state machine. Situational reasoning tracks transitions between optimal drive, static hold, and turning maneuvers. State constraints enforce even-keel balance, vetoing actions like backing water during turns to prevent structural singularity and maximize hydrodynamic glide.

primitives.name: Swings Out Operator
primitives.verbatim_quote: Swings out," that is, fails to keep in line over the keel so that the men are not in line.
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: x_i(t): transverse displacement (m), v_i(t): transverse velocity (m/s)
primitives.assumptions: Continuous differentiable motion along the slide; rigid body approximation for the oarsman.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Singularity occurs when transverse deviation exceeds the lateral stability margin, causing catastrophic loss of stroke power.

layer2.mapping: Isomorphic to transverse phase drift in coupled oscillator networks. Represents a breakdown in spatial symmetry relative to the central momentum vector.
layer2.telemetry: High-frequency IMU lateral acceleration variance across the crew.

primitives.name: Gets In Late Operator
primitives.verbatim_quote: Gets in late." The oar goes into the water after the others, or the swing up with the shoulders is too slow and breaks the time.
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: \Delta t: temporal lag (s), \omega: angular velocity of shoulder swing (rad/s)
primitives.assumptions: A globally synchronized metronome exists; water entry requires a minimum threshold angular velocity.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Breakdown when \Delta t exceeds the recovery window, resulting in a clipped stroke and zero propulsive impulse.

layer2.mapping: Maps to temporal desynchronization in distributed control systems. A delayed trigger event disrupts the collective force integration kernel.
layer2.telemetry: Oarlock pressure sensor timestamp delta relative to the coxswain's cadence signal.

primitives.name: Gets Out Late Operator
primitives.verbatim_quote: Gets out late." The oar drags at finish and backs water.
primitives.assumptions: Fluid dynamics remain quasi-steady; blade exit angle dictates drag coefficient.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Singularity where backward drag force equals forward thrust, halting boat momentum entirely.

layer2.mapping: Represents a negative feedback loop in the propulsion cycle. Isomorphic to braking friction introduced post-impulse in a ballistic trajectory.
layer2.telemetry: Post-exit blade hydrodynamic resistance measured via strain gauges on the oar shaft.

reasoning_traces.retrocausal_genealogy: Walter Camp's early 20th-century codification of rowing terminology represents one of the earliest attempts to discretize continuous biomechanical flows into actionable diagnostic primitives. Historically, this lineage traces back to the classical mechanics of the 18th century, where Euler and Lagrange formalized the dynamics of rigid bodies and constrained systems. Camp's vernacular—'short on catch,' 'clips'—is the empirical precursor to modern motor learning theory and stochastic optimal control, translating complex differential equations into intuitive, coachable state failures.
reasoning_traces.theory_of_mind: In a competitive racing environment, these primitives become tools for adversarial modeling. A coxswain or opposing strategist observes the micro-failures of an enemy crew—such as a starboard side consistently 'getting in late.' Recognizing this asymmetry allows the opposing agent to adjust their pacing strategy, perhaps initiating a sprint when the rival's synchronization is most fragile. The decision actor must infer the hidden fatigue states of the opposing oarsmen from these visible kinematic degradations, predicting exactly when the crew will cross the threshold into catastrophic desynchronization.
